Q: How to add ldapPublicKey schema to 389DS A:
  1. Imported user entries should the sshPublicKey attribute as text instead of binary data

The attributes show as binary data because that's how you defined them – octetStringMatch is meant for binary data and this influences how Apache Directory Studio renders the attribute.

Given that SSH public keys are ASCII strings (well, UTF-8 strings to allow for the comment), the attribute should rather have caseExactMatch as its equality rule.

(You can add custom overrides in Apache Directory Studio preferences, but better define the attribute right in the first place.)

It would also be a good idea to have SUBSTR caseExactSubstringsMatch as that would allow you to search e.g. for all users that have an obsolete DSA key using (sshPublicKey=ssh-dss*). Without an SUBSTR(INGS) matching rule, this would always give 0 results.

  1. Adding a new attribute does not show sshPublicKey as an available attribute

  2. Adding a new entry from scratch does not show ldapPublicKey as a structural class

This is a client issue. Being able to add the user entry at all indicates that the attribute schema definition is loaded into the server.

In Apache Directory Studio, connect to your server, then go to "LDAP → Open Schema Browser" and click the yellow "Reload Schema" button in the top-right corner. The app caches the schema upon first connection and does not automatically detect changes.


Also, your descriptions are wrong because an auxiliary objectClass is by definition not mandatory, and an attribute by itself cannot decide whether it is mandatory or not (some objectClasses can have it as MUST while other objectClasses can have it as MAY at the same time).

"Service that accepts LDAP public keys" also doesn't really make sense given that 1) it deals with SSH public keys and not LDAP public keys (which would be X.509 certificates); 2) it lets you define entities that have public keys, which has nothing to do with whether those entities accept keys.

Q: Regular Expression to test if input is an ok substring from the pattern A:

You could write your regex like this:

(fo?o?|ba?r?).

If the list of words doesn't change often and isn't large, that might be a good solution. Is the list of words is rather dynamic, you might want to check if an entry.starstWith(yourInput).

Q: How do you translate (+) joins when they appear across multiple tables? A:

Your query rewrite is correct. Some join conditions are superfluous in your query, but they were already superfluous in the original query.

The inner joins force A.COL_1 = B.COL_1 = C.COL_1, hence one of the following three conditions is enough.

AND A.COL_1 = D.COL_1(+)  
AND B.COL_1 = D.COL_1(+)
AND C.COL_1 = D.COL_1(+)

The inner joins also force B.COL_2 = C.COL_2, so one of the following two conditions is also sufficient.

AND B.COL_2 = D.COL_2(+)
AND C.COL_2 = D.COL_2(+)

Your query is correct and you can remove some join conditions, just as you could have done in the original query. Joining with USING instead of ON makes this even simpler and very easy to read:

SELECT *
FROM      a
JOIN      b USING (col_1)
JOIN      c USING (col_1, col_2)
LEFT JOIN d USING (col_1, col_2);

(This only works, though, if table A has no col2. This is usually the case, for you seem to be joining on composite natural keys here, so it would make no sense for the other tables to have these columns, too. And the result set will have less columns than your queries, because duplicate columns get removed when joining with USING.)

Q: Windows Form IsClosing flag? A:

How about using the event Form.FormClosing Event

The FormClosing event occurs as the form is being closed. When a form is closed, it is disposed, releasing all resources associated with the form. If you cancel this event, the form remains opened. To cancel the closure of a form, set the Cancel property of the FormClosingEventArgs passed to your event handler to true.
